arml-2008-power-01a.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. Compute the number of ways a $1\times4$ rectangle can be tiled with $1\times1$ and $1\times2$ tiles.

arml-2008-power-01b.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. Give two different tilings of a $12\times15$ rectangle with combinations of $2\times4$ and $3\times3$ tiles.
arml-2008-power-01b.answer: Two tilings: a $12\times12$ block of $2\times4$ tiles beside a $12\times3$ strip of four $3\times3$ tiles, with the strip on the right in one tiling and on the left in the other.

arml-2008-power-01c.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. Prove that it is impossible to tile an $80\times80$ rectangle with tiles of sizes $3\times11$ and $4\times15$.
arml-2008-power-01c.answer: Area argument mod 3 (or the top-row Diophantine equation $11j+15k=80$).

arml-2008-power-02a.prompt: Let $S(n)$ be the set of tilings of a $1\times n$ rectangle with $1\times1$ and $1\times2$ tiles (tiles cannot be rotated; e.g. a $1\times3$ rectangle has $2$ tilings with one $1\times1$ and one $1\times2$ tile, plus $1$ with three $1\times1$ tiles). For $n\in\{1,2,\dots,10\}$, compute the number of tilings. Give your answers in a table.

arml-2008-power-02b.prompt: Let $S(n)$ be the set of tilings of a $1\times n$ rectangle with $1\times1$ and $1\times2$ tiles. Determine, with proof, a recursive formula for $|S(n)|$. Use the formula to compute the number of ways to tile a $1\times17$ rectangle.

arml-2008-power-03a.prompt: In a table, list all values of $n\le40$ such that a $1\times n$ rectangle can be tiled with $1\times10$ and $1\times12$ tiles. For each such $n$, list a combination of $10$'s and $12$'s that works.

arml-2008-power-03b.prompt: A $1\times n$ rectangle can be tiled with $1\times10$ and $1\times12$ tiles for some values of $n$. Compute the number of values of $n$ with $1000\le n\le2008$ for which this is possible.

arml-2008-power-03c.prompt: Let $S(n)$ be the set of tilings of a $1\times n$ rectangle with $1\times2$ and $1\times3$ tiles. Determine, with justification, a recursive formula for $|S(n)|$, and then compute the number of ways to tile a $1\times17$ rectangle.

arml-2008-power-04a.prompt: For this question only, suppose $1\times1$ tiles are gray and $1\times2$ tiles are colored in two ways: the right half white and the left half black, or vice versa. Thus there are two distinct types of $1\times2$ tiles. Using these colored tiles, determine the number of distinguishable tilings for a $1\times17$ rectangle. Explain the method used.

arml-2008-power-04b.prompt: For this question only, suppose $1\times1$ tiles are gray and $1\times2$ tiles are colored in two ways: the right half white and the left half black, or vice versa (two distinct types of $1\times2$ tiles). Using these colored tiles, give an explicit, closed-form (non-recursive) formula in terms of $n$ for the number of distinguishable tilings of a $1\times n$ rectangle. Justify your formula.

arml-2008-power-05.prompt: Find, with justification, the number of different ways to tile an $8\times8$ rectangle using $2\times2$ and $1\times3$ tiles (a $1\times3$ tile is $1$ high and $3$ wide and cannot be rotated). It is not necessary to use both types in a tiling.

arml-2008-power-06a.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. Prove that if an $m\times n$ rectangle can be tiled with $u_1\times v_1$ and $u_2\times v_2$ tiles, then $m\in\langle u_1,u_2\rangle$ and $n\in\langle v_1,v_2\rangle$, where $\langle a,b\rangle=\{at_1+bt_2:t_1,t_2\ \text{nonnegative integers}\}$.
arml-2008-power-06a.answer: Read the tile heights down the left edge and the tile widths along the top edge.

arml-2008-power-06b.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. Give an example to show that the condition $m\in\langle u_1,u_2\rangle$ and $n\in\langle v_1,v_2\rangle$ is not sufficient to guarantee the existence of a tiling of an $m\times n$ rectangle with $u_1\times v_1$ and $u_2\times v_2$ tiles.

arml-2008-power-07.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. The *complexity* of a tiling is the smallest number $c\ge1$ of sub-rectangles, each tiled with copies of a single tile, into which the tiled rectangle can be divided. Assume neither tile is a scaled copy of the other, i.e. $\frac{u_1}{u_2}\ne\frac{v_1}{v_2}$. Under what conditions on $u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2,m$ and $n$ does an $m\times n$ rectangle have a tiling of complexity $1$ when $u_1\times v_1$ and $u_2\times v_2$ tiles are used? Justify your answer.
arml-2008-power-07.answer: Exactly when ($u_1\mid m$ and $v_1\mid n$) or ($u_2\mid m$ and $v_2\mid n$).

arml-2008-power-08.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. The *complexity* of a tiling is the smallest number $c\ge1$ of sub-rectangles, each tiled with copies of a single tile, into which the tiled rectangle can be divided. Assume neither tile is a scaled copy of the other, i.e. $\frac{u_1}{u_2}\ne\frac{v_1}{v_2}$. Under what conditions on $u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2,m$ and $n$ does an $m\times n$ rectangle have a tiling of complexity at most $2$ when $u_1\times v_1$ and $u_2\times v_2$ tiles are used? Justify your answer.
arml-2008-power-08.answer: Complexity $2$: $m\in\langle u_1,u_2\rangle$, $n\in\langle v_1,v_2\rangle$ and either ($u_1\mid m$ and $u_2\mid m$) or ($v_1\mid n$ and $v_2\mid n$). Complexity at most $2$: that, or the complexity-1 conditions of Problem 7.
arml-2008-power-08.reviewNote: The book states the condition for complexity exactly 2 and omits the complexity-1 case that 'at most 2' also requires; both are given here.

arml-2008-power-09.prompt:
Let $R$ be an $m\times n$ rectangle, where $m$ and $n$ are not necessarily integers, colored in a checkerboard pattern with squares of size $\frac12\times\frac12$ (starting with a black square in the corner). You may assume as a lemma that if a $u\times v$ tile is placed on $R$ with edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle, and at least one of $u$ and $v$ is an integer, then the tile covers equal areas of black and white.

Prove that if $R$ is tiled with two different kinds of tiles, where each kind of tile has at least one integral dimension, then at least one of $m$ and $n$ is an integer.
arml-2008-power-09.answer: Show that if neither $m$ nor $n$ is an integer, $R$ has unequal black and white areas, contradicting the lemma.

arml-2008-power-10.prompt: Given a rectangle whose dimensions are $a\times b$ ($a,b$ integers), a *tiling* by rectangular tiles of integer dimensions $u_1\times v_1,u_2\times v_2,\dots$ is an arrangement of tiles that fills the rectangle with no gaps and no overlaps, with tile edges parallel to the sides of the rectangle. A $u\times v$ tile has height $u$ and width $v$; tiles cannot be rotated, and two tiles of the same dimensions are indistinguishable. The *complexity* of a tiling is the smallest number $c\ge1$ of sub-rectangles, each tiled with copies of a single tile, into which the tiled rectangle can be divided. Assume neither tile is a scaled copy of the other, i.e. $\frac{u_1}{u_2}\ne\frac{v_1}{v_2}$. Use the following result (Problem 9): if a rectangle with non-integer dimensions is tiled by two kinds of tiles each having at least one integral dimension, then at least one of its dimensions is an integer (this holds for any real $m,n$ and any tiles with an integral side). If $u_1,v_1,u_2,v_2,m$ and $n$ are all positive integers, and an $m\times n$ rectangle $R$ can be tiled with tiles of dimensions $u_1\times v_1$ and $u_2\times v_2$, prove that it has a tiling with those tiles of complexity at most $2$.
arml-2008-power-10.answer: Scale the tiling to use tiles with a side equal to $1$, apply Problem 9 twice, and combine with Problem 8.
